10-15 min on ice. Slices of electric organ (15-20 g) are finely chopped with a scalpel until the macroscopic structure of the tissue is no longer visible. The mince is suspended in 200 ml of Torpedo physiological medium consisting of: 280 mM NaCl, 3 mM KCl, 1.8 mM MgCl₂, 3.4 mM CaCl₂, 1.2 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 6.8), 5.5 mM glucose, 300 mM urea, and 100 mM sucrose. When equilibrated with 0₂, NaHCO₃ (4-5 mM) is added to adjust the solution to pH 7.0-7.1. All further steps are carried out in a cold room at +4°C. After stirring for 30 min (magnetic stirrer), the suspension is forced through stainless steel grids, which were purchased from Tripette et Renaud (Paris, France). Grids (3 cm diam.) are stuck, by heating, to the openings of 50-ml plastic syringes whose ends have been sawed off. The suspension is successively passed through three grids with square openings of 1,000-, 500-, and 200-μm side length. After each step, the tissue adherent to the grid is recovered by scraping it off with a scalpel blade. The suspension is then filtered through a nylon gauze (50-μm square openings) under slight suction. The nylon cloth is washed with 50 ml of physiological medium. The filtrate (fraction F) is then centrifuged at 6,000 g for 20 min. The supernate (fraction S) is discarded. The pellet (fraction P) is resuspended in 20-25 ml of physiological medium and vigorously shaken. Then 6 ml of P are layered onto a discontinuous sucrose gradient prepared 1¹/₂-2 h before. This gradient has already been described in a previous report (22). The fractions obtained are, from the top to bottom of the tube: a clear supernate (A), three bands at each interface (B, dense; C, wider; D, hazy), and a thick pellet (E).
Incubation of Synaptosomes
Fraction C (40 ml, when prepared from six gradients) is twice diluted in the physiological medium without sucrose. The synaptosomes are allowed to warm up to 20°C for 15 min. Two precursors of ACh are used: [1- $^{14}$ C]acetate (Amersham CFA 13, specific radioactivity 58 mCi/mmol, Amersham/Searle Corp., Arlington Heights, Ill.), methyl- $[^{14}$ C]choline (Amersham CFA 424, specific radioactivity 58 mCi/mmol) at a final concentration of 1 μCi/ml, or methyl- $[^{3}$ H]choline (Amersham TRK 179, specific radioactivity 10.1 Ci/mmol) at a final concentration of 5 μCi/ml. Unlabeled acetate or choline is added to the incubation medium as indicated for each experiment. At the end of the incubation period, samples are subjected to filtration. Millipore filters (0.65 μm, MF Millipore DAWP 02500, Millipore Corp., Bedford, Mass.) are placed into filtration chambers (Swinnex 25, SX 0002500, Millipore Corp.) mounted on 10-ml syringes. Filtration is performed by suction under vacuum. Before a 1-ml sample of synaptosomes is passed through it, the filter is saturated with 1 ml of 10 mM unlabeled precursor in the physiological medium. Then the filter is washed with 10 ml of physiological medium kept in ice. The filter is dried on What-
man 42 paper and then extracted immediately in ice-cold solvent.
Extraction Procedure
Extraction of acetyl-labeled ACh is achieved by dissolving the filter in 3 ml of allyl cyanide containing Na $^{+}$ -tetraphenylborate (10 mg/ml). Total radioactivity is measured in an aliquot of 1 ml. The remaining 2 ml are washed in 8 ml of Na-phosphate buffer (10 mM, pH 7.4). After centrifugation, the organic phase is collected and counted. The specificity of the procedure when applied to the electric organ has been tested (23).
Extraction of choline-labeled ACh
is achieved by dissolving the filter in 2 ml of ethylbutylketone containing Na $^{+}$ -tetraphenylborate (10 mg/ml).

Ethylbutylketone serves as the organic solvent, while sodium tetraphenylborate acts as a selective precipitating agent. In this context, tetraphenylborate ions have a high affinity for choline derivatives, causing them to precipitate out of the solution as a solid, while other compounds remain dissolved. This section details the methods used to quantify specific enzymes and metabolites, providing a biochemical profile of the tissue samples.
Choline acetyltransferase (EC 2.3.1.6) is measured as described by Fonnum (13).
This enzyme is the rate-limiting step in the synthesis of acetylcholine, making its activity a key indicator of cholinergic function.
Acetylcholinesterase (EC 3.1.1.7) is measured by the method of Ellman et al. (10).

This enzyme breaks down acetylcholine, and its activity is crucial for terminating synaptic signals. The Ellman method is a standard colorimetric assay that allows for precise quantification of this hydrolytic activity.
Lactate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.27) is determined as described by Johnson and Whittaker

This is a bioassay method where the tissue extract is applied to a muscle preparation, and the resulting contraction is measured. The use of eserine (an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor) ensures that the ACh is not broken down before it can act on the muscle receptors, allowing for a sensitive detection of the neurotransmitter.
ATP is measured by the luciferine-luciferase method (34) using a photomultiplier unit built in the laboratory (Meunier & Lesbats, unpublished method).

This bioluminescent assay is highly sensitive and specific for ATP. The reaction involves the enzyme luciferase catalyzing the oxidation of luciferin, which emits light proportional to the amount of ATP present. The use of a custom-built photomultiplier unit suggests a high level of sensitivity and control over the measurement conditions, tailored to the specific needs of this study.

Free ACh measured in total tissue (23) or in minced tissue (31) was found to be 2.8 times more radioactive than bound ACh. Therefore, ACh compartmentation is maintained in purified and incubated synaptosomes.

To understand the significance of this finding, we must first define what is meant by "compartmentation." In the nervous system, acetylcholine (ACh) is not simply dissolved uniformly throughout the cell. Instead, it is packaged into specific, membrane-bound containers called synaptic vesicles. This separation is crucial for the precise timing of neurotransmitter release. The data above demonstrates that even after the nerve endings (synaptosomes) have been physically isolated from the tissue and subjected to the stress of freezing and thawing, this internal organization remains intact. The fact that the "free" ACh (the neurotransmitter outside the vesicles) is significantly more radioactive than the "bound" ACh (the neurotransmitter inside the vesicles) indicates that the vesicles are still acting as distinct, sealed compartments. They have not leaked their contents into the surrounding cytoplasm, preserving the functional architecture necessary for normal nerve signaling.

DISCUSSION
Validity of the Isolation Procedure
The journey to obtaining these pure nerve endings was not straightforward.
As pointed out by Sheridan et al. in 1966 (33),
attempts to fractionate the electric organ failed “to concentrate nerve endings or synaptic vesicles in any one fraction . . .”

This initial difficulty highlights a common challenge in cell biology: biological tissues are complex mixtures, and separating specific components without destroying them is akin to trying to separate the seeds from the pulp of a fruit without crushing the seeds.
Although further efforts succeeded in isolating synaptic vesicles (20, 21, 36), a nerve ending fraction, i.e., synaptosomes, was not available until 1976 (22).
Synaptosomes are essentially the presynaptic terminals of neurons, sealed off from the rest of the cell. They are the "business end" of the nerve where neurotransmitters are stored and released.
Early observations had indeed shown that, when electric tissue was homogenized in sucrose (33, 19) or glycine (19, 21), the presynaptic membrane sequestered a few vesicles.

Homogenization is a mechanical process that breaks tissue into small pieces, and the use of specific sugar solutions (sucrose or glycine) helps create density gradients that allow different cellular components to separate based on their weight.

Recently, the glycine and sucrose-glycine media were re-used in an attempt to purify these particles—called T-sacs by Dowdall et al. (3) and Dowdall and Zimmerman (6). Unfortunately, these authors have not yet published a detailed description of the isolation procedure or of their fraction.
This lack of transparency makes it difficult for other researchers to replicate their work, a significant hurdle in scientific progress.
Michaelson and Sokolovsky (30), using similar but $Ca^{++}$ -free media, described in a preliminary account a method for preparing synaptosomes.

The exclusion of calcium ions ($Ca^{++}$) is a critical detail here. Calcium is a key trigger for neurotransmitter release; by removing it, the researchers aimed to prevent the nerve endings from releasing their contents prematurely during the isolation process. However, their method had drawbacks.
These particles are recovered at an interface where they are likely to be associated with free synaptic vesicles and soluble choline acetyltransferase diffusing from the supernate.

Choline acetyltransferase is the enzyme responsible for synthesizing ACh. If this enzyme leaks out of the synaptosomes and mixes with the surrounding liquid (the supernate), it contaminates the sample, making it difficult to study the enzyme's activity specifically within the nerve endings.
This disadvantage should be overcome by adding an intermediate layer between the supernate and their fraction.

Such a layer would act as a barrier, preventing the diffusion of soluble enzymes into the synaptosome fraction.

Furthermore, the
leakage curve of ACh (30% in 30 min) renders the synaptosomes isolated by Michaelson and Sokolovsky inconvenient for metabolic studies.

A 30% loss of neurotransmitter in just half an hour means the "container" is leaking. For metabolic studies, which often take several hours to observe changes in synthesis or breakdown, a stable, sealed system is essential. If the ACh leaks out, the measurements become unreliable.
By using physiological media and mild mechanical comminution of the electric tissue, we were able to overcome most of the difficulties pointed out above.

"Physiological media" refers to a solution that mimics the natural ionic environment of the body, maintaining the correct salt concentrations and pH to keep the cells alive and functional. "Mild mechanical comminution" means gently breaking the tissue apart rather than using aggressive forces that could damage the delicate nerve endings.
The fractionation procedure described is rapid ( $2^{1/2}-3$ h are necessary for the whole procedure).
Speed is another advantage; the faster the isolation, the less time the cells have to degrade or lose their integrity.

and morphological analysis. The nerve endings remain in physiological media during the whole process. After dilution and warming, they retain all their ACh and choline acetyltransferase for at least 3 h so that metabolic studies are possible.

This stability is the key improvement over previous methods. By retaining both the neurotransmitter and the enzyme that makes it, the synaptosomes remain a functional, self-contained unit. This allows researchers to study the actual metabolic processes of ACh synthesis and release in a controlled environment.
The yield of the procedure is not very high, since we can estimate that we isolate 5–10% of the nerve endings of the tissue.
In other words, for every 100 nerve endings in the original tissue, only 5 to 10 are successfully recovered in the final fraction. While this might seem low, it is a deliberate trade-off.
Because the starting material is abundant and richly innervated, we have not tried to increase the yield at the expense of purity.

In scientific research, a small amount of high-quality, pure data is often far more valuable than a large amount of contaminated data. Purity ensures that the results are truly due to the properties of the synaptosomes and not artifacts from other cell types.

Synthesis of ACh by Synaptosomes

precursors and incorporate them efficiently into ACh. The rate of synthesis is linear for at least 2 h, and maximum incorporation rates are reached for concentrations of choline or acetate of about 100 $\mu$ M. More radioactive choline than acetate accumulates in the synaptosomes, but the rate of acetate incorporation into ACh is twice that of choline. This might be explained by a dilution of radioactive choline into an endogenous pool. Of particular interest is the observation that up to 90% of the incorporated acetate is converted to ACh. Since the tetraphenylboron extraction procedure is specific of quaternary ammonium (12), it is easy to separate precursor and product. The high percentage of conversion makes acetate a valuable precursor for studying the synthesis and release of ACh. Kinetic parameters for choline uptake are similar to those determined by other authors (see Results). It is of interest to notice that acetate is also taken up by an apparent high affinity process. As for intact or minced tissue, labeled ACh in synaptosomes represents only a few percent of the total ACh after several hours of incubation under resting conditions.

The definitions of free ACh is operational. It represents the difference between total ACh and ACh bound to vesicles that can be isolated and observed in electron microscopy. Free ACh might represent the cytoplasmic pool where ACh synthesis occurs or a pool associated with fragile vesicles which have still to be characterized. Whatever free ACh means, it represents a physiologically active compartment directly involved during stimulation of the electric organ (7-9). It is interesting to find, as for intact tissue or minces (31), that this compartment represents $\sim 40\%$ of the total ACh content of synaptosomes and that its specific radioactivity is about 2.5 times that of bound, i.e., vesicular, ACh. These results were obtained regardless of the disruption procedure used: homogenization (intact tissue) or freeze-thawing (synaptosomes). Both procedures respect the integrity of synaptic vesicles.

The present work demonstrates that it is possible to obtain synaptosomes from the electric organ of Torpedo by selecting an adequate disruption procedure. The resulting fraction is pure and exclusively cholinergic and therefore represents a useful tool for further studies. The good physiological preservation of the synaptosomes and their stability in vitro permit the labeling of the transmitter. Acetate appears to be a suitable precursor for further studies on synthesis and release of ACh. Because of its high purity and the absence of postsynaptic elements, this fraction is a good starting material for the isolation of homogeneous presynaptic membranes.
